1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3.strategy: The main line: it supports d4 with a pawn, so that after ...cxd4 cxd4 the chain is intact and Black is as cramped as before. It takes c3 from the queen's knight, and Black has to bring more pressure with pieces if the d4-pawn is to be undermined.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3.strategy: Defends d4 and e5 with a piece instead of a pawn, so White develops and keeps c3 in reserve. After a capture on d4 White usually does not retake at once but castles first. The d4-pawn is less firmly supported than after c3, so the game gets sharper.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch System

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.b4.strategy: A gambit: the b-pawn is offered to drag the c-pawn away from the attack on d4 and open lines on the queenside, for example for the c1-bishop to reach a3. Black takes it with ...cxb4 and is a clean pawn up; White must prove the open lines are worth it.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.b4.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Frenkel Gambit

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Qg4.strategy: Hits g7 and e6 at once and aims for a quick kingside initiative, at the cost of the d4-pawn. But the f8-bishop covers g7, the queen is out early, and after ...cxd4 Black is simply a pawn up.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Qg4.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch Attack

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.dxc5.strategy: Takes the pawn and so hands Black what it wants: the d4-pawn that anchored the chain is gone, and e5 is left without its base. Black recovers the pawn with ...Bxc5 while developing, and White has only released the pressure on Black's centre.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.dxc5.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Steinitz Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6.name: French Defence: Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds a second attacker to d4 beside the c5-pawn, while also eyeing e5. Black does not trade on d4 yet: it keeps up the pressure on the base of the chain with pieces and makes White find enough defenders.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Qb6.strategy: Puts the queen behind the c-pawn, where it joins the pressure on d4 once the c-pawn captures and hits b2 along the b-file. It also prepares to trade Black's bad bishop on b5, a respectable alternative to developing the knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn, undermining the base of the chain. White usually answers by developing the bishop rather than retaking at once, so Black has an extra pawn to look after against a lead in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Qg4 cxd4.strategy: Accepts the offered pawn: g7 is covered by the f8-bishop and e6 by the f7-pawn and the c8-bishop, so the queen's sortie has no immediate target, and Black is simply a pawn up.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Paulsen Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3.strategy: The main line: the knight defends both d4 and e5, so d4 now has three defenders against Black's two attackers. White develops and keeps the whole chain together, accepting that the centre stays under pressure and that Black decides how to increase it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Be3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Kupreichik Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Be3.strategy: Adds a defender to d4 with a developing move, but takes the bishop away from the b2-pawn: 5...Qb6 at once attacks the undefended pawn, so White has to spend a move on it. A rarely played sideline that wins no advantage.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.strategy: The most common move: the queen adds to the pressure on d4 and attacks b2, which the c1-bishop cannot leave without dropping the pawn. That makes d4 hard to defend with pieces alone. Black commits the queen early, and White has to decide how to meet the pressure.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 B.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Euwe Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 B.background: Greco mentioned 5...Bd7 as early as 1620. It is known as the Euwe Variation and was popularised by Viktor Korchnoi in the 1970s; it is now a main line.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 B.strategy: The bad bishop develops at once and the queen keeps its best square open, so White must show its plan first. It gives up the direct pressure on b2, but White's usual a3 is then a wasted move, because Black can use the time to strike at the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Main Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.background: In current theory this is the most important line of the Advance Variation.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.strategy: The most important line today: it takes b4 from Black's pieces and prepares b4 itself, which would gain queenside space and free the c1-bishop from guarding the b2-pawn. The move is slow, so Black gets time to decide how to fight the expansion.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Milner-Barry Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.background: Named after Stuart Milner-Barry, a chess player and wartime codebreaker whose name is attached to four opening variations.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.strategy: Sacrifices the d4-pawn for development and an attack: White gets open lines and a lead against the uncastled king. Black has to defend accurately, as grabbing d4 with both knight and queen walks into Bb5+, a check that uncovers an attack on the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Lputian Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Q.strategy: Heads for f5 to attack d4, keeping the f8-bishop's diagonal open. White can double Black's pawns by taking on h6, but that gives up the c1-bishop and opens the g-file, which is considered fine for Black. A respected alternative.

Accepts the gambit and takes the pawn. Black must then watch the b5-square, because grabbing d4 a second time with the knight loses the queen to Bb5+. The extra pawn is real, but White's lead in development means Black has to defend accurately.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Qb6 5.Nf3.strategy: The natural reply: the knight develops and defends d4 and e5, keeping the pawn chain intact. White need not fear the queen on b6 yet, since the c1-bishop guards b2.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Qb6 5.Nf3 B.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Wade Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Qb6 5.Nf3 B.background: Named after Robert Wade, who first played it in 1953 against Enrico Paoli. It came into widespread use from 1955 and has since been played by some of the strongest players in the world, including Anatoly Karpov, Yasser Seirawan and Levon Aronian.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Qb6 5.Nf3 B.strategy: Brings out the bad bishop with the aim of trading it on b5 for White's light-squared bishop, the queen on b6 supporting the exchange there. The plan costs time, since Black spends moves on the bishop and later on the queen's position, so the trade has to be worth it.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3 cxd4 5.Bd3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Ruisdonk Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Nf3 cxd4 5.Bd3.strategy: Offers the pawn for development: the bishop comes out and White castles, leaving the knight on f3 to guard e5 instead of retaking at once. White gets a lead in development, but Black has a clean extra pawn to defend with.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Qg4 cxd4 5.Nf3.name: French Defence: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.Qg4 cxd4 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on the d4-pawn while the queen keeps g7 and e6 under fire. White is a pawn down for the moment, and Black has to meet the kingside threats before consolidating, but the compensation is doubtful.
